issue.title: Migrate to Musl

labels.name: repo-f8f539ca
labels.description: Developement process & source code & implementation details

labels.name: repo-f8f539ca
labels.description: Build system (CMake, compilation, platform builds).

issue.body:
### Company or project name

ClickHouse

### Use case

ClickHouse can already be built with Musl, and we have made numerous efforts to make it possible and for it to pass the CI checks.

See the motivation below.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Advantages:

1. Different systems can have slightly different versions of glibc. While we fully control the ClickHouse code, we don't control glibc. Certain versions of glibc can contain bugs, and it can be difficult to debug. See example here: https://sourceware.org/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=25847

2. When using glibc, the behavior of a program can be controlled by LD_PRELOAD, LD_LIBRARY_PATH, and similar environment variables, and it represents a security vulnerability or confusion in an attempt to alter the program's behavior with these variables. See examples here https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/43933 and https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/36340 

3. While controlling our own libc, we can build it with better instrumentation. At the same time, glibc on different systems can be built with or without frame pointers, and sometimes the CFI information can be miscompiled, or use unsupported DWARF extensions.

4. One of the biggest advantages is "bring your own libc" - we can modify it and rebuild any time. This will make it simpler to implement hooks for certain functions, or to remove unused and dangerous parts of libc, or implement runtime audit and instrumentation. Example here: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/18711

5. There is no need to support the "glibc_compatibility" and "harmful" libraries.

6. Running the binary in chroot or Docker will require less number of extra files (no need to copy .so). The same applies when running a cross-built binary under QEMU-user. The same applies when running ClickHouse on weird Linux distributions such as Alpine.

7. Open the path for migration to llvm-libc (which does not exist still) or Cosmopolitan libc (which is not ready for production usage with C++ apps).


Caveats:

1. Certain functions in Musl are implemented in assembly without proper stack unwinding information (CFI directives). We will have to write the missing directives manually to get proper stack traces.

2. There are rumors that the DNS resolver in Musl is somehow worse than in glibc.

3. Musl has a lower thread stack size by default, and we will have to implement some workaround for that.

4. The math library in Musl is slower, and we will have to provide different implementations for those functions.

5. There is a chance that mutexes or thread creation will be slower.


Plan:

We have to get rid of the remaining usage of `dlopen`. Currently, it is used only in `clickhouse-odbc-bridge` and `clickhouse-library-bridge`. The proposal is to take out their code from the codebase and put it in a separate repository (similar to `clickhouse-copier`), then make the final release of these tools, and forget.


### Describe alternatives you've considered

Alternatively, we will do the preparations, remove `clickhouse-odbc-bridge` and `clickhouse-library-bridge`, remove `dlopen`, but keep using glibc.

### Additional context

issue.title: GCS INSERTs with s3_create_new_file_on_insert fail for files over 32 MiB

labels.name: repo-f8f539ca
labels.description: Object storage connectivity (S3/GCS/Azure) including credentials, retries, multipart, etc.

issue.body:
### Describe what's wrong

- Every INSERT to GCS with `s3_create_new_file_on_insert = 1` fails once the object exceeds `s3_max_single_part_upload_size` (32 MiB default).
- Triggered by any INSERT producing a multipart upload, even the first write to a fresh key, no concurrent writer needed.
- Expected both INSERTs to succeed and write two separate numbered files.
- On an `S3` table the later `SELECT` then 404s on the key that was never written.

Root cause: `StorageObjectStorageSink` sets `object_storage_write_if_none_match = "*"` for every backend except HDFS, so `WriteBufferFromS3::preFinalize` throws for a GCS client whenever the upload must go multipart, a guard added separately for small Iceberg metadata objects.

<details>
<summary>Analysis details (evidence, affected locations, impact)</summary>

Why we believe this is a bug: `StorageObjectStorage::write` -> `StorageObjectStorage::createSink` passes `fail_if_exists = create_new_file_on_insert && !truncate_on_insert` (StorageObjectStorage.cpp:1109; partitioned path: StorageObjectStorageSink.cpp:198). The sink then sets `object_storage_write_if_none_match = "*"` for every backend except HDFS (StorageObjectStorageSink.cpp:76-77). On finish, `StorageObjectStorageSink::finalizeBuffers` -> `WriteBufferFromS3::finalizeImpl` -> `preFinalize`, which throws for a GCS-provider client whenever a conditional create is not a single PUT (WriteBufferFromS3.cpp:188-192).

Affected locations:
- [`src/Storages/ObjectStorage/StorageObjectStorageSink.cpp:76`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/8a8d2e477fc/src/Storages/ObjectStorage/StorageObjectStorageSink.cpp#L76) — conditional write requested for every backend but HDFS
- [`src/Storages/ObjectStorage/StorageObjectStorage.cpp:1109`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/8a8d2e477fc/src/Storages/ObjectStorage/StorageObjectStorage.cpp#L1109) — createSink passes fail_if_exists for create_new_file_on_insert without truncate
- [`src/Storages/ObjectStorage/StorageObjectStorageSink.cpp:198`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/8a8d2e477fc/src/Storages/ObjectStorage/StorageObjectStorageSink.cpp#L198) — partitioned sink passes the same fail_if_exists
- [`src/IO/WriteBufferFromS3.cpp:188`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/8a8d2e477fc/src/IO/WriteBufferFromS3.cpp#L188) — GCS client throws on a conditional create that is not a single PUT

Impact: On master, every GCS export or append with `s3_create_new_file_on_insert = 1` that produces a file larger than 32 MiB fails, even with no concurrent writer. This worked on 26.10. The error does not point to the workaround (`s3_max_single_part_upload_size` above the file size, which buffers the whole object in memory). Unreleased: neither change is on 26.3/26.8, and 26.10.3.7 writes the files.

</details>

### Does it reproduce on most recent release?

Confirmed on `master`; not checked on a release.

### How to reproduce

Reach MinIO under the hostname storage.googleapis.com so the S3 client detects the GCS provider, then INSERT roughly 40 MB of data to exceed the single-part upload size.

```bash
import pytest

from helpers.cluster import ClickHouseCluster

cluster = ClickHouseCluster(__file__)
node = cluster.add_instance("node", with_minio=True)

@pytest.fixture(scope="module")
def started_cluster():
    try:
        cluster.start()
        # The S3 client deduces the GCS provider from the endpoint, so reach MinIO under the GCS host name.
        node.exec_in_container(
            ["bash", "-c", f"echo '{cluster.minio_ip} storage.googleapis.com' >> /etc/hosts"],
            privileged=True,
            user="root",
        )
        yield cluster
    finally:
        cluster.shutdown()

def test_create_new_file_on_insert_multipart_gcs(started_cluster):
    url = f"http://storage.googleapis.com:{cluster.minio_port}/{cluster.minio_bucket}/gcs_new_file"
    creds = f"'{cluster.minio_access_key}', '{cluster.minio_secret_key}'"
    # About 40 MB, more than `s3_max_single_part_upload_size`: the object is uploaded in parts.
    insert = f"INSERT INTO FUNCTION s3('{url}.csv', {creds}, 'CSV', 's String') SELECT repeat('a', 1000) FROM numbers(40000)"

    node.query(insert)
    node.query(insert, settings={"s3_create_new_file_on_insert": 1})

    assert node.query(f"SELECT _file, count() FROM s3('{url}*.csv', {creds}, 'CSV', 's String') GROUP BY _file ORDER BY _file") == "gcs_new_file.1.csv\t40000\ngcs_new_file.csv\t40000\n"
```

### Expected behavior

Both INSERTs succeed and the SELECT lists `gcs_new_file.csv` and `gcs_new_file.1.csv` with 40000 rows each.

Expected output of the reproducer above:

```
Both INSERTs succeed and the final SELECT returns:
gcs_new_file.1.csv	40000
gcs_new_file.csv	40000
(26.10.3.7 writes `export.csv` and `export.1.csv` with 40000 rows each for the same INSERTs.)
```

### Error message and/or stacktrace

The second INSERT throws S3_ERROR: GCS conditional create must be a single PUT, CompleteMultipartUpload ignores preconditions.

Actual output of the reproducer above:

```
helpers.client.QueryRuntimeException: Client failed! Return code: 243, stderr: Received exception from server (version 26.11.1):
Code: 499. DB::Exception: Received from 172.18.0.6:9000. DB::Exception: GCS conditional create of gcs_new_file.1.csv must be a single PUT. CompleteMultipartUpload ignores preconditions.. Stack trace:
[frames 0-3 trimmed]
5. src/IO/WriteBufferFromS3.cpp:189:15: DB::WriteB
```

<details>
<summary>Suggested fix</summary>

Two options:
- Treat a GCS client like HDFS when the upload goes multipart: fall back to an unconditional `CompleteMultipartUpload` for the `*_create_new_file_on_insert` sink instead of throwing. Trade-off: large GCS files lose the overwrite protection #114995 (where this was found; not confirmed as the cause) adds, which is the 26.10 behaviour.
- Exclude GCS in the sink altogether. Trade-off: small GCS files also lose the `x-goog-if-generation-match: 0` single-PUT protection.

</details>

### Additional context

Open risks:
- If both #114995 and #128866 are backported, the regression goes with them.
- Other S3-compatible stores that reject `If-None-Match` on PUT or CompleteMultipartUpload would now fail these INSERTs too. Could not verify: only MinIO and the GCS client path were exercised.

Found during automated review of [PR #114995](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114995); this finding was not executed, so nobody is tagged. Per git blame, that PR introduced the cited lines (src/Storages/ObjectStorage/StorageObjectStorage.cpp:1109, src/Storages/ObjectStorage/StorageObjectStorageSink.cpp:198). Severity P2 · Finding `h_pr114995_001`

Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/130064


### Changelog category (leave one):
- Build/Testing/Packaging Improvement


### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md):
A CMake re-run no longer rewrites unchanged generated files (`TimeZones.generated.cpp`, `StorageSystemLicenses.generated.cpp`, the LLVM `.def` headers and the musl `bits/*.h` headers), so it no longer recompiles the code that uses them, and it configures faster: `git status` skips the work trees of submodules and `list-licenses.sh` no longer forks per vendored Rust crate.

### Description

Based on part (d) of patch 2 by snelheidai in #130064.

Every CMake re-run rewrote some configure-time outputs even when their content did not change, so ninja recompiled their dependents: 20 TUs in a debug build (`TimeZones.generated.cpp`, the 13 MB licenses source, 18 LLVM/`CHJIT.cpp` TUs), and almost everything in a musl build, because `bits/alltypes.h` is on every compile's `-isystem` path. The new `write_file_if_changed()` in `cmake/utils.cmake` writes a temporary file and copies it with `file(COPY_FILE ... ONLY_IF_DIFFERENT)`; the licenses source is copied the same way. Configure time also went to a `git status` that scans all submodule work trees (now `--ignore-submodules=dirty`; the configure log no longer lists modified content inside submodules) and to a license script that forked about 10 processes per crate.

Two changes against the posted patch: its `process_library` shortcut drops `libxml2`, `rapidjson` and `sz3` from `system.licenses` under mawk, the awk of the CI builder image, so the shortcut here is equivalent under any awk; and the helper does not use `file(READ)`, which drops the `\r` of a CRLF line end.

Validation, debug build, ccache, `touch CMakeLists.txt`, median of 4 runs:

| | master | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `ninja build.ninja` | 18.5 s | 7.4 s |
| `ninja clickhouse` | 62.3 s | 52.4 s |
| TUs compiled | 20 | 0 |
| musl build dir, `ninja _lz4` | 1682 compiles | 0 |

The generated files, `system.licenses` and the `list-licenses.sh` output (gawk and mawk) are byte-identical to master. The `ninja clickhouse` gain is smaller than the saved compiles because master re-runs the Rust archive post-processing on every build (part (a) of #130064).

issue.body: ### Company or project name _No response_ ### Describe what's wrong I found this issue while running 26.8.1.2041 on prod, leaked accumulated over 1 month, but reproduced at 26.8.36.3. I used Claude to debug the issue, and it found is reported as: # JIT: `compiled_expression_cache_size` does not bound JIT memory; `LLVMContext` grows unbounded with distinct literals until `SYSTEM DROP COMPILED EXPRESSION CACHE` When `compile_expressions = 1` and the workload sends many queries whose filter expressions embed different literals (for example `(device_id = 1 AND ts > '...') OR (device_id = 2 AND ts > '...') OR ...` generated by a client), JIT memory grows linearly with the number of compiled functions and is never released, even though `CompiledExpressionCacheBytes` stays pinned at `compiled_expression_cache_size` and entries are being evicted. `jemalloc.jit_arena.active_bytes` grows about 30x faster than the bytes accounted by the cache. The growth is proportional to the number of literals in the expression (0.78 MiB/compile at 250 OR-clauses, 0.02 MiB/compile at 25), which points at the constants and types interned by the single `LLVMContext` for its whole lifetime (as noted in #104113). Evicting a cache entry frees the module's code pages but not what the context interned, and nothing resets the context automatically; only `SYSTEM DROP COMPILED EXPRESSION CACHE` (which recreates the JIT instance) returns the memory. In production (26.8.1.2041, 30 GiB pod, a BI client issuing ~600 such queries/hour) the server's idle `MemoryTracking` grew ~0.45 GiB/day from 0.75 GiB to 17.8 GiB over five weeks, until unrelated queries started failing with `MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` (total). `system.jemalloc_bins` showed 15.3 GiB in 3.2M objects of the 5120-byte bin. Days with zero `CompileFunction` events showed zero growth. Setting `compile_expressions = 0` for that user stopped the growth. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes ### How to reproduce Reproduced on 26.8.1.2041, 26.8.36.3, 26.10.2.103 and 26.11.1.1328 (head, `clickhouse/clickhouse-server:head`). Note: on 26.10+ the planner moves the filter of the query below into PREWHERE under `FINAL` and that path is not compiled, so the exact query no longer triggers it; `optimize_move_to_prewhere = 0` (or any shape that keeps the filter as a compiled `Filter` step) reproduces it identically. `compiled_expression_cache_size` lowered to 2 MiB so eviction starts quickly (the default 128 MiB behaves the same, just later): ```bash cat > small-cache.xml <<'EOF' 2097152 EOF docker run -d --name chjit -p 18123:8123 \ -v $PWD/small-cache.xml:/etc/clickhouse-server/config.d/small-cache.xml \ clickhouse/clickhouse-server:26.10.2.103 ``` ```python # python3 repro.py http://127.0.0.1:18123 [n_queries=800] [n_clauses=250] import random, sys, time, urllib.request, urllib.parse URL, N, NCL = sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 800, int(sys.argv[3]) if len(sys.argv) > 3 else 250 def q(sql, **s): req = urllib.request.Request(f"{URL}/?{urllib.parse.urlencode(s)}", data=sql.encode()) return urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=300).read().decode().strip() def stats(label): time.sleep(1.5) arena = int(q("SELECT value FROM system.asynchronous_metrics WHERE metric = 'jemalloc.jit_arena.active_bytes'")) cache, cnt = (int(q(f"SELECT value FROM system.metrics WHERE metric = '{m}'")) for m in ("CompiledExpressionCacheBytes", "CompiledExpressionCacheCount")) tracked = int(q("SELECT value FROM system.metrics WHERE metric = 'MemoryTracking'")) compiles = q("SELECT value FROM system.events WHERE event = 'CompileFunction'") or "0" print(f"{label:<14} compiles={compiles:>5} jit_arena={arena/2**20:8.1f}MiB cache={cache/2**20:4.1f}MiB/{cnt:<4} MemoryTracking={tracked/2**20:8.1f}MiB", flush=True) def query(rnd): conds = " OR ".join(f"(device_id = {rnd.randrange(5000)} AND ts > '2026-10-{rnd.randrange(1, 5):02d} " f"{rnd.randrange(24):02d}:{rnd.randrange(60):02d}:{rnd.randrange(60):02d}')" for _ in range(NCL)) return f"SELECT device_id, issue.title: Parts with any skip index written by 26.8+ are unreadable and unmergeable on 26.6 after a rollback: `Unknown format (1) of packed data (UNKNOWN_FORMAT_VERSION)`

labels.name: repo-f8f539ca
labels.description: Skipping indexes (minmax, set, bloom) and their evaluation.

issue.body:
Any data part that 26.8 or newer writes for a table with at least one skip index (even a single `minmax`) cannot be used by 26.6 after a rollback: `count()`, every `SELECT` with a `WHERE` (also on the primary key, also with `use_skip_indexes = 0`), every merge, and the rows of `system.parts` / `system.columns` for that table fail with `Code: 287. DB::Exception: Unknown format (1) of packed data. (UNKNOWN_FORMAT_VERSION)`. Only a full scan without a filter still works. The failure is not only in index analysis: `IMergeTreeDataPart::calculateColumnsAndSecondaryIndicesSizesOnDiskUnlocked` opens the archive to compute column sizes, which the planner asks for on almost every query. Merges stay blocked until the server is upgraded again, so the partition keeps accumulating parts. No data is lost: the table works again after upgrading back to 26.8.

The packed skip-index archive `skp_idx.packed` was added in 26.6 behind `packed_skip_index_max_bytes` (default 0) with archive index format version 0 (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/105321). In 26.7, https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109272 added a per-file `uncompressed_size` field to the archive index and made the skip-index writer always use the new format version 1 (`PackedFilesIO::VERSION_WITH_UNCOMPRESSED_SIZE`, `src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeDataPartWriterOnDisk.cpp`, the `finalize` call of `skip_indices_packed_writer`); `statistics.packed` and packed part storage keep writing version 0. In 26.8, https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111816 enabled packing by default (`packed_skip_index_max_bytes = 1 MiB`), so from 26.8 on practically every part with a skip index carries a version 1 archive. The 26.6 reader (`PackedFilesReader::readIndex` in `src/IO/PackedFilesReader.cpp`) rejects anything above `PackedFilesIO::VERSION = 0`; it cannot just skip the new field, because each index entry is now 8 bytes longer. `26.6` (latest 26.6.1.2475 included) has no backport of the reader change. The 26.8 changelog entry for https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111816 states that the new parts "stay fully readable on older versions", which is not true for 26.6.

26.8 and 26.10 read each other's archives (both use format version 1, `MAX_VERSION = 1`), and master (26.11) archives read fine on 26.10 and 26.8. Only 26.6 is affected.

```bash
d=$(mktemp -d)
clickhouse-26.8 local --path $d -q "
    CREATE DATABASE d ENGINE = Atomic;
    CREATE TABLE d.t (id UInt64, v UInt64, INDEX i v TYPE minmax GRANULARITY 1) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id;
    INSERT INTO d.t SELECT number, number FROM numbers(1000)"
ls $d/store/*/*/all_1_1_0/ | grep skp_idx          # skp_idx.packed, first byte 0x01
clickhouse-26.6 local --path $d -q "SELECT * FROM d.t WHERE id = 5 SETTINGS use_skip_indexes = 0"
# Code: 287. DB::Exception: Unknown format (1) of packed data. (UNKNOWN_FORMAT_VERSION)
clickhouse-26.6 local --path $d -q "SELECT count() FROM d.t"
# Code: 287. DB::Exception: Unknown format (1) of packed data. (UNKNOWN_FORMAT_VERSION)
clickhouse-26.6 local --path $d -q "INSERT INTO d.t SELECT number, number FROM numbers(10); OPTIMIZE TABLE d.t FINAL"
# Code: 287. DB::Exception: Unknown format (1) of packed data. (UNKNOWN_FORMAT_VERSION)
clickhouse-26.6 local --path $d -q "SELECT sum(v) FROM d.t"
# 499545 (a full scan without a filter still works)
```

The 26.8 side can avoid it: with a server-level `compatibility` below 26.8 (`clickhouse-26.8 local --compatibility=26.6`, or `compatibility` in the default profile on a server) the `MergeTree` default becomes `packed_skip_index_max_bytes = 0`, parts get the standalone `skp_idx_<name>.idx2` / `.cmrk4` files, and 26.6 reads them. A session-level `SET compatibility = '26.6'` does not help, because `MergeTree` settings come from the server-level default profile. Parts already written with a version 1 archive stay unreadable on 26.6.

Expected: a 26.8 part with a skip index is readable on 26.6, as the changelog promises. Proposed fix: backport the read side of https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109272 to `26.6` (accept index format version 1 in `PackedFilesReader::readIndex` and read, or skip, the `uncompressed_size` field). It is a few lines and does not change what 26.6 writes. Also correct the 26.8 changelog entry.

A server-level `compatibility` below 26.8 restores `packed_skip_index_max_bytes = 0` and avoids the problem; a session-level `compatibility` does not.

Found by the upgrade/rollback harness, `26.6 -> 26.8 -> 26.6`.

@groeneai please fix this.

issue.title: Native ORC reader decodes Nullable(Float32/Float64) values byte by byte; one copy makes these reads 30-44% faster

labels.name: repo-f8f539ca
labels.description: Input/output formats (CSV/JSON/Parquet/ORC/Arrow/Protobuf/etc.).

issue.body:
### Describe the situation
The native ORC reader decodes each non-null value of a `Nullable(Float32)`/`Nullable(Float64)` column byte by byte. On ARM this made `formats_columns_nullable` #52 24% slower in CI. Reading the non-null values with one copy and moving them to their rows in place makes such reads 30-44% faster.

Mean of 20 warm runs per round, 8 paired rounds, clickhouse-local on Graviton3 (4 vCPU), `max_threads = 1` unless noted.

| Query / workload | Baseline | Patched | Change (95% CI) |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `formats_columns_nullable` #52, `min`/`max` of `Nullable(Float32)` | 19.30 ms | 13.21 ms | -31.5% (-32.4% .. -30.7%) |
| `formats_columns_nullable` #84, `Nullable(Int32)` + `Nullable(Float64)` | 44.22 ms | 30.91 ms | -30.1% (-30.5% .. -29.7%) |
| `formats_columns_nullable` #4, `SELECT *` | 279.6 ms | 260.3 ms | -6.9% (-7.1% .. -6.8%) |
| `min`/`max` of `Nullable(Float64)`, same file | 31.14 ms | 17.34 ms | -44.3% |
| 10M rows, `Nullable(Float32)` + `Nullable(Float64)` with NaN, Inf, -0, denormals | 406.0 ms | 237.2 ms | -41.6% |
| same, `max_threads = 4` | 400.1 ms | 231.9 ms | -42.0% |
| same, cold (page cache dropped, new process), median of 6 | 659 ms | 490 ms | -25.8% |
| #52 cold, median of 6 | 165.0 ms | 158.5 ms | -4.1% |
| Control: #20, `avg` of `Nullable(Int32)` | 8.98 ms | 8.97 ms | -0.1% (-0.6% .. +0.3%) |
| Peak RSS, 10M-row query x3 | 264-281 MB | 264-265 MB | unchanged |

<details><summary>Why it happens and what the patch changes</summary>

`FloatingColumnReader::next` in `src/Processors/Formats/Impl/ORC/ColumnReader.cpp` copies a column without nulls with one `readBytes`. With nulls it runs `out[i] = not_null[i] ? read() : 0`, and `read()` builds each value from 4 or 8 `InputByteStream::readByte()` calls, each checking for the end of the buffer. In a profile of #52 this function takes 41% of the time.

The patch counts the non-null values, reads them with one `readBytes` into the start of the output, and then moves them to their rows from the back, writing 0 for nulls as before. The k-th non-null value goes to a row i >= k, so no value is overwritten before it is moved. On big-endian hosts only the values read are byte-swapped. The unused `read()` is removed. The no-null path, `skip` and seeking are unchanged.

The regression came with #127690: `formats_columns_nullable` #52 went from 25.7 ms to 31.8 ms in the ARM per-commit run of its merge (f0a51f60f29) and stayed there in the nightly runs. The x86 per-commit run of the same merge did not flag #52 (22.6 ms to 21.7 ms), while #84 rose 8% (69.4 ms to 74.7 ms) in the ARM nightly run of 2026-11-02 and stayed there. The test writes the ORC file with each server's own writer. Swapping writers and readers between the official builds of b1e2520f04f and f0a51f60f29 shows that the slowdown is in the reader: 15.0 ms with the old reader and 17.0 ms with the native one, whichever build wrote the file.

Correctness: for files written by the native writer, digests of the row ids, null flags and exact float bits match the source MergeTree tables for 10M rows with NaN, +-Inf, -0 and denormals, long runs of nulls, all nulls, no nulls, the `formats_columns_nullable` table, and `Array`/`Map`/`Tuple`/`Array(Array)` of nullable floats. The full `SELECT *` of the `formats_columns_nullable` file is identical between the builds, and all 20 ORC files under `tests/` read identically (4 of them fail the same way in both builds).

</details>

### Which ClickHouse versions are affected?
<details><summary>Tested versions and source commits</summary>

Master since #127690 (26.11). Measured on master da712df1be649f13b1958cfb1de60acc069fca54 (26.11.1.1); the ORC reader is unchanged up to 39b9f2d5aedb4e405d37df3f4037b749c4912dd5. Both builds: Release, clang-21, no ThinLTO, same build tree, on AWS Graviton3 (Neoverse-V1, 4 vCPU). x86 was not measured.

</details>

### How to reproduce
<details><summary>Data, queries and measurement procedure</summary>

Create the source table of `tests/performance/formats_columns_nullable.xml` (1M rows) and write it once as ORC:

```sql
-- the CREATE TABLE source_table and INSERT INTO source_table ... FROM numbers(1000000) of formats_columns_nullable.xml, then:
INSERT INTO FUNCTION file('fcn.orc', 'ORC') SELECT * FROM source_table;
```

The 10M-row file:

```sql
CREATE TABLE corr (id UInt64, f32 Nullable(Float32), f64 Nullable(Float64)) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id;
INSERT INTO corr SELECT number,
    multiIf(k = 0, NULL, k = 1, nan, k = 2, inf, k = 3, -inf, k = 4, -0., k = 5, toFloat32(1e-42), toFloat32(number) / 7),
    multiIf(k2 = 0, NULL, k2 = 1, nan, k2 = 2, -inf, k2 = 3, 5e-324, k2 = 4, -0., number / 3.)
FROM (SELECT number, cityHash64(number) % 9 AS k, cityHash64(number, 1) % 7 AS k2 FROM numbers(10000000));
INSERT INTO FUNCTION file('corr.orc', 'ORC') SELECT * FROM corr;
```

Queries, each with `SETTINGS max_threads = 1 FORMAT Null`:

```sql
SELECT min(if(isNull(col_float32), 0, col_float32)), max(if(isNull(col_float32), 0, col_float32)) FROM file('fcn.orc', 'ORC');  -- #52
SELECT sum(ifNull(col_int32, 0)), avg(ifNull(col_float64, 0)) FROM file('fcn.orc', 'ORC') GROUP BY intDiv(id, 1000000);       -- #84
SELECT * FROM file('fcn.orc', 'ORC');                                                                                        -- #4
SELECT avg(col_int32) FROM file('fcn.orc', 'ORC');                                                                           -- #20
SELECT min(col_float64), max(col_float64) FROM file('fcn.orc', 'ORC');
SELECT sum(f32), sum(f64) FROM file('corr.orc', 'ORC');  -- also with max_threads = 4
```

Procedure: one `clickhouse local --time --queries-file` process per build and round; each query runs 21 times and the first run is dropped; the round value is the mean of the other 20. 8 rounds alternate the order of the builds. Cold: drop the page cache before a new process with one query, 6 rounds.

</details>

### Expected performance
<details><summary>Expected behavior</summary>

Nullable floating-point columns should be read about as fast as non-nullable ones: the data stream holds only the non-null values, which can be copied at once as the no-null path already does.

</details>

### Related issues and pull requests
<details><summary>Related work</summary>

https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/127690
https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/129345

</details>

### Additional context
<details><summary>Full patch</summary>

```diff
diff --git a/src/Processors/Formats/Impl/ORC/ColumnReader.cpp b/src/Processors/Formats/Impl/ORC/ColumnReader.cpp
index 318acd41ceb..7b0f641188a 100644
--- a/src/Processors/Formats/Impl/ORC/ColumnReader.cpp
+++ b/src/Processors/Formats/Impl/ORC/ColumnReader.cpp
@@ -156,8 +156,20 @@ public:
             return;
         }
 
+        /// Read the non-null values with one copy, then move each one to its row, from the back:
+        /// the k-th non-null value goes to a row i >= k, so it is never overwritten before it is moved.
+        size_t num_not_null = 0;
         for (size_t i = 0; i < num_values; ++i)
-            out[i] = not_null[i] ? read() : 0;
+            num_not_null += not_null[i] != 0;
+
+        stream->readBytes(reinterpret_cast<char *>(out), num_not_null * sizeof(ItemType));
+        if constexpr (std::endian::native == std::endian::big)
+            for (size_t i = 0; i < num_not_null; ++i)
+                out[i] = std::bit_cast<ItemType>(std::byteswap(std::bit_cast<Bits>(out[i])));
+
+        size_t k = num_not_null;
+        for (size_t i = num_values; i-- > 0;)
+            out[i] = not_null[i] ? out[--k] : 0;
     }
 
     void seekToRowGroup(std::unordered_map<UInt64, PositionProvider> & positions) override
@@ -169,14 +181,6 @@ public:
 private:
     using Bits = std::conditional_t<sizeof(ItemType) == 8, UInt64, UInt32>;
 
-    ItemType read()
-    {
-        Bits bits = 0;
-        for (size_t b = 0; b < sizeof(ItemType); ++b)
-            bits |= static_cast<Bits>(stream->readByte()) << (b * 8);
-        return std::bit_cast<ItemType>(bits);
-    }
-
     std::unique_ptr<InputByteStream> stream;
 };
 
```

@groeneai could you take a look? If the analysis and patch hold up, feel free to open a PR if it fits.

</details>

issue.title: Background column-TTL merge wedges forever when a dependent MATERIALIZED column throws on the reset default (regression from #117815)

labels.name: repo-f8f539ca
labels.description: Confirmed user-visible misbehaviour in official release

labels.name: repo-f8f539ca
labels.description: TTL rules and TTL merges (moving/recompressing/rolling-up/deleting parts).

labels.name: repo-f8f539ca
labels.description: MergeTree* family: parts, merges, primary index, column statistics, background data transformation.

issue.body:
A background column-TTL merge permanently wedges when a dependent `MATERIALIZED` column's expression throws on the source column's default value (e.g. `intDiv(100, x)` when the TTL resets `x` to `0`). Introduced on master by #117815: the recompute added there runs inside the TTL merge with no error isolation, so every background merge throws, retries forever, parts accumulate without bound, and the TTL is never applied — with no user action and nothing surfaced to the client.

### How to reproduce

ClickHouse master `26.10.1.1231` (commit `bee127a4800f`). A plain `MergeTree`, no user command involved after `INSERT`:

```sql
CREATE TABLE t_bg
(
    d DateTime,
    x Int32 TTL d + INTERVAL 3 SECOND,
    m Int32 MATERIALIZED intDiv(100, x)
)
ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple()
SETTINGS min_bytes_for_wide_part = 0, merge_with_ttl_timeout = 1;

INSERT INTO t_bg (d, x) VALUES (now(), 5);
INSERT INTO t_bg (d, x) VALUES (now(), 7);
-- wait a few seconds for the column TTL to expire and a background merge to be scheduled
```

Once the TTL expires, the background TTL merge resets `x` to its default `0` and then recomputes `m = intDiv(100, 0)`, which throws. The server log fills with:

```
<Error> MergeTreeBackgroundExecutor: Exception while executing background task {...::all_1_2_1}:
Code: 153. DB::Exception: Division by zero: while executing 'FUNCTION intDiv(100 :: 1, x :: 0) -> intDiv(100, x) Int8 : 3': While executing TTL. (ILLEGAL_DIVISION)
```

The merge is retried indefinitely. Inserting more rows shows parts accumulating and never merging, and the TTL is never applied (`x` is never reset):

```sql
SELECT count() FROM system.parts WHERE table = 't_bg' AND active;  -- grows without bound
SELECT x, m FROM t_bg ORDER BY x;                                  -- x never reset to 0
```

In a 60-second run with 6 inserts this produced 6 active parts that never merged and 194 logged merge failures. Eventually the table hits `TOO_MANY_PARTS` and becomes unwritable.

### Expected

The background TTL merge makes progress: a dependent `MATERIALIZED` column whose recompute throws on the reset default must not permanently wedge the merge queue or block the column TTL from being applied.

### Bug and control on the same build

Same server, same binary `26.10.1.1231`:

- Bug arm `m MATERIALIZED intDiv(100, x)`: background merge throws forever, parts accumulate, TTL never applied, 194 failures.
- Control `m MATERIALIZED x + 1`: background merge succeeds, parts merge to one, `x` reset to `0`, `m` recomputed to `1`, zero failures.

Pre-fix control on released `26.10.1.1` (before #117815): the TTL merge resets `x` and does **not** recompute `m`, so there is no throw and merges proceed (the pre-fix behavior #117310 reported as "stale `m`"). The wedge is new on master.

### Root cause

#117815 (merged `3b05333210f2`, closing #117310) added `MATERIALIZED`-column recompute to the column-TTL merge path in `src/Processors/Transforms/TTLTransform.cpp`. `recomputeDependentColumns` (around line 292) calls `ITTLAlgorithm::executeExpressionAndGetColumn` with no `try`/`catch`, and the dependent-column filter in `analyzeDependentMaterializedColumns` (lines ~88-112) excludes only non-deterministic expressions and columns in the sorting / primary / partition key — not expressions whose domain excludes the source column's default. Any common partial-domain expression (`intDiv`, `%`, out-of-range `arrayElement`, etc.) over a TTL-reset column therefore turns a previously-working table into a silently wedged one.

### Impact

Unbounded part growth and a stuck TTL on a table that was valid at creation and worked for every `INSERT`, `SELECT`, and merge until the TTL expired — triggered automatically by the passage of time, with no user action and no error returned to any client. The only signal is the server error log. Distinct from the user-initiated `ALTER TABLE ... CLEAR COLUMN` recompute, where the same expression throws synchronously and visibly to the caller.

issue.body:
C and C++ are compiled with `-fstack-protector-strong`, but the Rust crates had no equivalent: e.g. the Rust `brotli::enc::literal_cost::BrotliEstimateBitCostsForLiterals` allocates ~6 KiB of stack without a canary, while the C implementation of the same routine has one.

- Pass `-Zstack-protector=strong` to Rust, next to the C/C++ flag and with the same fuzzer exclusion.
- Enable `-C overflow-checks=yes`: an integer overflow panics instead of wrapping silently, and the FFI boundaries (`catch_unwind`) already turn panics into errors.
- Always rebuild the Rust standard library with `-Zbuild-std` (previously only in sanitizer builds), so `std`/`core`/`alloc` get the same flags. This costs about 1.23x wall time on a clean Rust-only build (279 s vs 227 s locally).
- Add `-C force-frame-pointers=yes` when `DISABLE_OMIT_FRAME_POINTER` is set, matching C/C++.
- Add `-Zub-checks=yes` in sanitizer builds only, since a violation aborts the process.

The performance impact of overflow checks is to be evaluated in the CI performance tests.

### Changelog category (leave one):
- Performance Improvement


### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md):
Without `GROUP BY`, `uniq`, `uniqExact`, `count(DISTINCT)`, `uniqHLL12`, `uniqTheta`, `min`, `max` and `groupUniqArray` of a `LowCardinality(String)` or `LowCardinality(FixedString)` column are faster when values repeat: each distinct value of a block is added once instead of every row (up to 14x faster for columns with few distinct values).


### Description

Closes #127916 (analysis by @ snelheidai).

`Aggregator::prepareAggregateInstructions` materializes every `LowCardinality` argument, so these functions copy and add every row, although a repeated value never changes their state.

Change: a new `IAggregateFunction::ignoresRepeatedValues()` (like `canOptimizeEqualKeysRanges`), true for `uniq`, `uniqExact`, `uniqHLL12`, `uniqTheta`, `groupUniqArray` and non-float `min`/`max` (a repeated `NaN` can replace a different `NaN`), forwarded by the `-Null` wrapper. Not for `uniqCombined`: its full exact set turns into HLL on any insert. Without keys, a single `LowCardinality(String|FixedString)` argument of such a function is kept when its dictionary has at most half the block rows, and the function gets only the used values in the order of their first occurrence, so the state is the same as after adding every row (also the `groupUniqArray` order).

The used values come from a new read-only `ColumnLowCardinality::getMinimalDictionary`: the same result as `getMinimalDictionaryEncodedColumn(...).dictionary`, but it stops once every key except the default and NULL has been seen, then looks for those two in the rest of the rows. Blocks of indexes that repeat the previous row (a sorted column) are skipped with a vector compare. A dictionary larger than the range keeps the old path. Functions of the same column share it per block, and the radix `uniqExact` from #127280 uses it too.

Validation, Release A/B, fix/base. 4 threads: 166 values with 94% `''` 0.24-0.50; 166 uniform values 0.07-0.23; `FixedString(16)` 0.17-0.49; `Nullable`, 90% NULL 0.46-0.60; 10000 values 0.66-0.89. The lookup alone, before/after, 1 thread, 30M rows: lone `uniqExact` (radix) 31 -> 17-20 ms, five functions of one column 93 -> 21-23 ms, an 8001-key dictionary used almost fully 40 -> 39-40 ms. 166 keys in runs of 50000 rows, 100M rows, 1 thread: 58 -> 28 ms with the skip. Mostly distinct values, numeric columns, `String`, `-If`, `GROUP BY`: unchanged. Results are identical.

issue.body:
The `quantileExact` family added values one row at a time, even without `GROUP BY`. This PR adds whole batches: a single copy for integers, `Decimal`, dates and floats without NaNs, and a branchless compaction when NaNs, NULLs or `-If` filter rows.

The batch path grows the array like `push_back` (doubling), not like `reserve` (power-of-two rounding). `deserialize` and `merge` into an empty state reserve the exact size.

Single thread, 320M-400M rows: 1.05x-1.19x faster depending on type and filter (`quantileExact(UInt64)` 1.17x, `quantileExactIf` 1.18x, `Nullable` with `-If` 1.19x). Peak memory is unchanged.

Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112827#issuecomment-6505643447
